nameStory: The tall evening primrose earned its name from its impressive height - it can tower up to 6 feet tall, making it one of the giants of the evening primrose family. Like its cousins, it's called an 'evening primrose' because its bright yellow flowers open in the evening hours, releasing their sweet fragrance to attract night-flying moths and other pollinators.
description: Tall evening primrose is a towering wildflower that can reach an impressive 6 feet in height, making it hard to miss when in bloom. This robust plant produces bright yellow flowers that open in the evening, filling the air with a sweet, lemony fragrance. It's a western North American native that occasionally appears in New England, where it grows as a tall, sturdy spike covered in cheerful blooms. The plant has a strong, upright growth habit with numerous flowers clustered along its impressive height.

idTips.label: Height
idTips.description: Dramatically tall plant reaching up to 6 feet - towers over most other wildflowers and is visible from a distance across meadows and roadsides

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with 4 petals that open in evening hours, releasing a sweet, lemony fragrance that's especially strong at dusk and dawn

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single tall, sturdy stem that shoots straight up with flowers clustered along the upper portion, creating a distinctive tower-like silhouette

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves that feel somewhat rough to the touch and are arranged alternately along the stem

habitat: In New England, this extremely rare visitor might be found along roadsides, in disturbed areas, or occasionally in moist meadows. It prefers areas with full sun and can tolerate a range of soil conditions from sea level to higher elevations.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and begin their rapid upward growth, developing the characteristic tall stem structure.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with bright yellow flowers opening each evening and releasing their sweet fragrance throughout warm nights.
seasonality.fall: Flowers may continue into early fall, followed by seed capsule development and eventual plant senescence.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely, leaving only seeds to potentially germinate the following season.

funFact: This plant is like a natural skyscraper of the wildflower world - at 6 feet tall, it can literally tower over a person's head, making it one of the tallest wildflowers you might encounter in North America!
confusionNotes: Its exceptional height makes it hard to confuse with other evening primroses, but if you're looking at a shorter specimen, check the bloom time - the evening opening and sweet fragrance are key clues that separate all evening primroses from day-blooming yellow wildflowers like goldenrods or sunflowers.
contextualKnowledge: With only one recorded observation in New England, this is essentially a botanical celebrity sighting if you encounter it - most evening primroses in our region are the shorter, more common species, making this towering western visitor extraordinarily rare.
compareHints: Unlike the common evening primrose which typically grows 3-5 feet tall, tall evening primrose can reach 6 feet, making it the giant of the genus. While common evening primrose is widespread in New England, tall evening primrose is extremely rare here - if you see a towering evening primrose, you're likely looking at something very special.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common evening-primrose is the tallest and most robust of New England's evening-primroses, with the largest flowers.
Small sundrops differs from its evening primrose relatives by staying low and sprawling rather than growing tall and upright like common evening primrose.
Among New England's evening primroses, northern evening primrose stands out for its smaller flower size compared to common evening primrose and Large-flowered evening-primrose.
Meadow evening primrose is much less common than its cousin common evening primrose, which grows much taller (3-6 feet) and has larger flowers that open in the evening.
Unlike the bold, large yellow flowers of common evening-primrose that can be 2 inches across, clockweed has tiny, delicate white or pink flowers only half an inch wide.
Unlike its yellow-flowered cousin common evening-primrose which grows tall and upright, pinkladies stays low and spreads horizontally.
Unlike its evening primrose cousins that typically have four-petaled yellow flowers opening at dusk, biennial beeblossom stands out with its pink flowers and incredibly tall, airy growth habit.
Unlike the tall, upright common evening primrose with its simple oval leaves, cutleaf evening primrose stays low to the ground with deeply divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Large-flowered evening primrose stands out from other Oenothera species primarily due to its impressive flower size - much larger than common evening primrose or the various sundrops species.
Among the many evening primroses in New England, red-stalked evening primrose stands out primarily for its reddish stem coloration, while most relatives like common evening primrose have green stems.
Bigfruit evening primrose stands out dramatically from its New England relatives like common evening primrose due to its sprawling, ground-hugging growth habit rather than upright stems.
Yellow sundrops differ from common evening-primrose by blooming during the day rather than evening and having distinctive blue-green waxy leaves instead of plain green ones.
Among the evening-primroses in New England, Nodding Evening-Primrose is unique for its drooping flower buds - all other species have upright, erect buds.
